Your response was: "Looked at it. Checkout flow. Nearly missed the submit button. It barely registered visually — took a moment to find the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "nearly missed the submit button", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The "Place Order" button is positioned below the more visually dominant "Continue Shopping" button, placing the primary action lower in the layout hierarchy where it draws less attention.

B) The "Place Order" button appears at the very bottom of the page with no surrounding whitespace or structural separation to distinguish it as the key action in the flow.

C) The "Continue Shopping" button occupies a larger, more prominent area directly above "Place Order", causing the secondary action to visually outrank the primary one in the layout.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
What kind of work situation typically brings you to a checkout layout like this one?
turns.a: Checkout flows. Time pressure. Need to submit quickly — can't afford to hunt for the submit button.

turns.q: When you scanned that checkout layout under time pressure, what were you trying to confirm about where the key action was positioned on the screen?
turns.a: Find and execute the primary CTA on the first scan. One look, one action. Not search and re-read to confirm it's available.

turns.q: If the "Place Order" button were repositioned in this layout, what would tell you at a glance that it had succeeded as the dominant action?
turns.a: 'Place Order' visible in under three seconds. Reads as active — high contrast, readable label. Execute it, confirmation appears. Zero scanning, zero re-reading to confirm it's available. That's the success state.

turns.q: When you look at the "Place Order" button in this layout, what is it about its actual appearance — its fill, color, or border style — that stops it from reading as the dominant action?
turns.a: 'Place Order' has gray fill on gray background, 12px label — reads as a disabled state. Not immediately identifiable as an active button. Had to scan past it and re-read to confirm it was even available. The affordance was wrong: inactive-looking styling on the primary action.
